How strongly does travel time shape where people register with a GP? This
guide answers that question for mainland Cornwall by fitting an allocation
model to the observed registrations. You will estimate how fast the pull of a
practice fades with travel time, compare each practice's modeled list (the
residents registered with it) with its observed list, check what the registrations can tell the model, see how much
the outside option adds, and save the results. The data are the bundled small
areas, practices, registrations and travel times described in [The Cornwall GP
example data](cornwall-data.html). The `spax()` interface and the allocation
model are experimental and may change in later versions.

The guide uses spax, with sf, dplyr and ggplot2 for tables and maps.

```{r packages, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(spax)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

## The model in words

The model shares the residents of each small area among the practices they
can reach. Each practice attracts residents in proportion to its supply, here
its GP full-time equivalents (FTE), discounted by the travel time from the
area. Residents can also take an outside option: here, registering with a
practice outside mainland Cornwall, in Devon or on the Isles of Scilly for
example. This is a conditional logit model (CLM). For small area $i$ and
practice $j$, the share of residents registered at $j$ is

$$P_{ij} = \frac{S_j \, w(d_{ij})}{\sum_k S_k \, w(d_{ik}) + v_0},$$

where $S_j$ is the GP FTE of practice $j$ and $d_{ij}$ the travel time in
minutes. The decay weight $w$ is 1 at zero minutes and falls with travel time.
This guide uses a Gaussian weight, $w(d) = \exp(-d^2 / 2\sigma^2)$, where the
travel scale σ, in minutes, sets how fast a practice's pull fades. The outside
weight v0 is the pull of the outside option, the same in every area, and the
outside share of an area is $v_0$ over the same denominator.

The shares over all practices and the outside option add up to 1, so a near
practice with many GP FTE draws residents away from the others. Demand, the
number of residents of an area, times these shares gives the modeled
registrations. Fitting finds the values of σ and v0 that bring the modeled
registrations closest to the observed ones. Closeness is measured by the
Poisson loss, the negative Poisson log-likelihood up to a constant. Lower is
better, only differences between fits to the same counts mean anything, and
the value itself can be negative.

## The data

The model needs demand by small area, supply by practice, the travel times
between them and the observed registrations. Demand is the residents of each
small area registered with any GP practice in England, and supply is GP FTE
excluding GPs in training. The recipe covers mainland Cornwall, because the
Isles of Scilly have no road link to the mainland. `prep_data()` lines up
demand, supply and travel by their IDs and records the units, and
`obs_flows()` reads the registrations from a long table with one row per small
area and practice.

```{r inputs}
areas <- cornwall_lsoa |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  st_drop_geometry()
gp <- cornwall_gp |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  st_drop_geometry()
travel <- cornwall_travel[areas$lsoa, gp$practice]
demand <- setNames(areas$registered, areas$lsoa)
supply <- setNames(gp$gp_fte_extg, gp$practice)
d <- prep_data(demand, supply, travel, metadata = list(
  demand_units = "registered residents", demand_period = "July 2026",
  supply_units = "GP FTE excluding GPs in training", supply_period = "June 2026",
  travel_units = "minutes"))
flows <- obs_flows(cornwall_flows, origin = "lsoa", facility = "practice", count = "patients")

d
flows
```

The data hold `r nrow(areas)` small areas and `r nrow(gp)` practices, with a
travel time for every pair (`unknown for 0 active origins`). The `policies`
line says that a missing demand or travel value would stop `prep_data()` with
an error. [Bringing your own data](data-prep.html) shows the alternatives for
missing travel times. `flows` lists the
`r format(nrow(cornwall_flows), big.mark = ",")` area-practice pairs with
registrations, and a pair it does not list counts as 0. The registrations are
a stock: who is registered where in July 2026, not a count of visits.

## Fit the model

`spec_clm()` specifies the model without data. By default the travel scale σ
of a Gaussian decay and the outside weight v0 are both `"fit"`, that is,
estimated from the observations. `spax()` fits the specification to the
registrations.

```{r fit}
clm <- spax(d, spec_clm(), observed = flows)
clm
```

```{r scilly-values, include = FALSE}
scilly_practices <- cornwall_gp$practice[cornwall_gp$scilly]
at_scilly <- sum(cornwall_flows$patients[
  cornwall_flows$lsoa %in% areas$lsoa &
    cornwall_flows$practice %in% scilly_practices
])
```

The message says what `spax()` left out when it lined the registrations up
with the data. One small area, on the Isles of Scilly, is not in the data, so
its registrations are dropped. Also, `r at_scilly` mainland residents are
registered at the Scilly practice, which is not in the data either. This fit
leaves them out. With `outside = "known"`, used in [When outside counts are
known](#when-outside-counts-are-known), they count as registered outside
mainland Cornwall.

The table lists the fitted σ and v0. `beta` and `kappa` are held at 1.
Attraction is `(kappa * supply)^beta`, so at 1 a practice attracts in
proportion to its GP FTE, the $S_j$ of the formula.

Fitting is a numerical search, and a search needs starting values. Without
them, `spax()` scans a grid of σ and v0 values (the `starts` line) and starts
the search from the best few grid points. The `selected` line says which
search gave the fit and how many converged. `boundary none` says that no
fitted value ended at the edge of its allowed range. `summary(clm)` lists
every start.

`coef()` returns the fitted values.

```{r coef}
coef(clm)
```

```{r sigma-values, include = FALSE}
sigma_hat <- coef(clm)[["sigma"]]
keep9 <- exp(-9^2 / (2 * sigma_hat^2))
```

The travel scale σ is about `r round(sigma_hat, 1)` minutes, so registration
is very local: a practice 9 minutes away, about twice σ, keeps only about
`r round(100 * keep9)`% of the pull it would have next door. The outside
weight v0, about `r signif(coef(clm)[["v0"]], 2)`, is on the scale of GP FTE.
The outside option pulls like a practice with that many GP FTE next door to
every area, so it matters only where no practice is near.

## Fitted against observed

`as.data.frame(clm, type = "flows")` gives one row per small area and practice,
with the modeled flow and the observed count. Summed by practice, they give
each practice's modeled and observed list of mainland residents.

```{r practice-fit, fig.width = 5, fig.height = 4.5, fig.alt = "Scatter plot of modeled against observed registered residents for the 54 mainland practices, in thousands, with a dashed equality line; the points scatter around the line, the largest practice lies well above it and a few practices lie well below it."}
flow_table <- as.data.frame(clm, type = "flows")

# Observed and modeled list of each practice
practices <- flow_table |>
  group_by(practice = facility_id) |>
  summarise(observed = sum(observed), modeled = sum(flow))
cor(practices$observed, practices$modeled)

ggplot(practices, aes(observed / 1000, modeled / 1000)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = 2, color = "gray50") +
  geom_point() +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(
    x = "Observed registered residents (thousands)",
    y = "Modeled registered residents (thousands)",
    title = "Practice lists from mainland residents"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r practice-values, include = FALSE}
fowey <- practices |>
  filter(practice == "L82035")
fowey_fte <- supply[["L82035"]]
st_austell <- practices |>
  filter(practice == "Y04957")
```

Modeled and observed lists correlate at
`r round(cor(practices$observed, practices$modeled), 2)`. The model knows only
GP FTE and travel time, so a practice with more registered patients per GP FTE
than its neighbors has a larger observed than modeled list and sits below the
dashed line. Fowey River Practice is the clearest case: it has
`r format(round(fowey$observed), big.mark = ",")` registered mainland residents
but `r round(fowey_fte, 2)` GP FTE excluding GPs in training, and the model
gives it `r format(round(fowey$modeled), big.mark = ",")`. The opposite holds
for the largest practice, St Austell Health Group, which sits well above the
line. The model gives it
`r format(round(st_austell$modeled), big.mark = ",")` residents against
`r format(round(st_austell$observed), big.mark = ",")` observed.

## What the data identify

Data identify a parameter when different values of it give clearly different
modeled counts, so that the observations can tell the values apart.
`check_fit()` asks whether the registrations carry information about distance
decay. It refits the model with distance decay switched off: every practice
with a travel time, here all `r nrow(gp)`, gets the same weight, so each area
splits its residents by GP FTE alone, with v0 fitted again. It compares the
two fits on the same loss and reports the one-way trips each fit implies.

```{r check}
check <- check_fit(clm)
check
```

```{r check-values, include = FALSE}
check_table <- as.data.frame(check)
fitted_row <- check_table[check_table$comparator == "fitted", ]
no_decay_row <- check_table[check_table$comparator == "no_decay", ]
```

Without distance decay the Poisson loss rises by
`r format(round(no_decay_row$loss_difference), big.mark = ",")`, and the
median trip grows from `r fitted_row$trip_median` to
`r no_decay_row$trip_median` minutes. `trip_p90` is the time within which 90%
of modeled trips fall. The flows record where each practice's patients live,
so they carry strong information about the decay. The `contact` column is the
share of demand that the model sends to a mainland practice.

The `capacity_only` comparator ignores where residents live: it sets each
practice's total in proportion to its GP FTE, with one fitted scale. It
applies only to fits to practice totals, so its row is `NA` here. [Reading
results](reading-results.html) explains how to read the check for those fits.

## When outside counts are known

The fit above sees only the counts at the mainland practices, so the outside
option has no count of its own. In Cornwall each area's outside count is
known. Demand counts every resident registered with any practice in England,
so the residents not registered at a mainland practice are exactly the outside
count: demand minus the counts at the mainland practices. `outside = "known"`
in `obs_flows()` declares this, and `spax()` then fits the outside count as one
more cell of each area. The chunk also compares the percent of residents
registered outside mainland Cornwall, observed and modeled by each fit.

```{r known-outside}
flows_known <- obs_flows(
  cornwall_flows,
  origin = "lsoa",
  facility = "practice",
  count = "patients",
  outside = "known"
)
clm_known <- spax(d, spec_clm(), observed = flows_known)
coef(clm_known)

# Percent of registered residents outside mainland Cornwall
outside_percent <- function(result) {
  by_area <- as.data.frame(result, type = "origins")
  100 * sum(by_area$demand * by_area$outside_share) / sum(by_area$demand)
}
known_areas <- as.data.frame(clm_known, type = "origins")
round(c(
  observed = 100 * sum(known_areas$outside_observed) / sum(known_areas$demand),
  `fit without outside counts` = outside_percent(clm),
  `fit with outside counts` = outside_percent(clm_known)
), 2)
```

The message now says that the counts at the Scilly practice are treated as the
outside option. The travel scale hardly moves
(`r round(coef(clm_known)[["sigma"]], 2)` against
`r round(coef(clm)[["sigma"]], 2)` minutes), while the outside weight rises
from `r signif(coef(clm)[["v0"]], 2)` to
`r signif(coef(clm_known)[["v0"]], 2)`. Without outside counts the fit
understates registration outside mainland Cornwall. With every outside count
known, the modeled total matches the observed one. When the outside counts are
known, as in Cornwall, the fit that uses them is the one to report: the next
section maps it, and [What if a practice closed?](scenario.html) builds on it.

Declare outside counts as known only when demand counts the same people as the
observations, as here: registrations by residence from one extract and date.
With a population estimate as demand, the gap between population and list
sizes would go straight into the outside counts: in mainland Cornwall the lists
exceed the mid-2024 population estimates by
`r round(100 * (sum(areas$registered) / sum(areas$pop) - 1), 1)`%.

## The outside option

The `"origins"` table of a result has one row per small area: its `demand`,
its modeled `outside_share` and `access`, the share of its residents modeled
at a mainland practice (1 minus the outside share; `check_fit()` reports the
demand-weighted mean of `access` as `contact`). A fit with outside counts
known adds `outside_observed`, each area's observed count outside mainland
Cornwall. The maps set the observed and modeled outside shares of `clm_known`
side by side.

```{r outside-map, fig.height = 3.5, fig.alt = "Two maps of mainland Cornwall's small areas. Observed: the share of residents registered outside mainland Cornwall is low almost everywhere and highest in a few areas in the north-east and east, along the Devon border. Modeled: a small share everywhere, highest in a few rural areas far from practices, such as in the north-east and at the western tip."}
# Observed and modeled outside shares by small area, in one long table
outside <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(
    lsoa = known_areas$origin_id,
    share = known_areas$outside_observed / known_areas$demand,
    source = "Observed"
  ),
  data.frame(
    lsoa = known_areas$origin_id,
    share = known_areas$outside_share,
    source = "Modeled"
  )
) |>
  mutate(source = factor(source, c("Observed", "Modeled")))

# Join to the small-area polygons for mapping
outside_map <- cornwall_lsoa |>
  select(lsoa) |>
  inner_join(outside, by = "lsoa")

ggplot(outside_map) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = 100 * share), color = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = st_union(outside_map), fill = NA, color = "gray20", linewidth = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~source) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    option = "mako",
    direction = -1,
    trans = "sqrt",
    name = "Registered\noutside (%)"
  ) +
  labs(title = "Share of residents registered outside mainland Cornwall") +
  theme_void()
```

```{r outside-values, include = FALSE}
observed_outside <- sort(known_areas$outside_observed, decreasing = TRUE)
top10_percent <- round(100 * sum(observed_outside[1:10]) / sum(observed_outside))
```

Observed registration outside mainland Cornwall is concentrated in a few areas
in the east, along the Devon border: the ten areas with the most residents
registered outside hold `r top10_percent`% of them. Many residents there are
probably registered with practices just across the border in Devon, which the
model does not include. The model has one outside weight for every area, so it
spreads a small outside share everywhere and puts its largest values where few
GP FTE lie within a short drive. Read the modeled outside share of a single
area as approximate.

`predict()` gives the same outputs for areas that were not fitted, from their
travel times to the practices and their demand. Run on the fitted areas, it
returns the outside shares of the `"origins"` table.

```{r predict}
prediction <- predict(clm_known, travel, demand, outputs = "outside_share")
prediction
all.equal(
  prediction$outputs$outside_share,
  setNames(known_areas$outside_share, known_areas$origin_id)
)
```

The print counts the origins whose values could be computed, here all
`r length(prediction$outputs$outside_share)`, and gives the range of each
output. `$outputs` holds the values, named by origin, and `$validity` the
status of each origin, for example `unknown_travel` for an area with an
unknown travel time.

## Without an outside option: the Huff model

Does the outside option earn its place? The Huff model answers by leaving it
out: every resident goes to a mainland practice. `spec_huff()` specifies it.
Its defaults are a power decay and a fitted attractiveness exponent (`beta`).
Here it takes the Gaussian decay and `beta = 1` of the conditional logit, so
the two fits differ only in the outside option.

```{r huff}
huff <- spax(d, spec_huff(decay = decay_gaussian(), beta = 1), observed = flows)
coef(huff)

# Loss differences are measured from the first fit, the Huff model
comparison <- compare_fits(list(huff = huff, clm = clm))
as.data.frame(comparison)[c("specification", "parameters", "loss_difference")]
```

```{r huff-values, include = FALSE}
compared <- as.data.frame(comparison)
outside_gain <- format(round(-compared$loss_difference[2], 1), nsmall = 1)
```

The Huff model is compared with `clm` because the two are fitted to the same
`flows`. Adding the outside option moves the travel scale very little (from
`r format(round(coef(huff)[["sigma"]], 3), nsmall = 3)` to
`r format(round(coef(clm)[["sigma"]], 3), nsmall = 3)` minutes) and lowers the
Poisson loss by `r outside_gain`. The Huff model is the conditional logit with
v0 fixed at 0, so this difference measures what the outside option adds on
these registrations. That is small next to the
`r format(round(no_decay_row$loss_difference), big.mark = ",")` that distance
decay adds in `check_fit()`: travel time does almost all the work.
Registrations are a stock rather than independent events, so read the loss as
a fitting criterion, not as the basis of a formal test.

## Keep the results

`as.data.frame()` turns a result into tables: `"parameters"`, `"facilities"`
(one row per practice), `"origins"` (one row per small area), `"flows"` and
`"starts"`. Save tables as CSV files for other software, and the whole result
as an RDS file, which keeps the specification, the data, the units and the
fit. The code saves `clm_known`, the fit to report.

```{r save}
# A temporary folder here; use your own, e.g. results_dir <- "results"
results_dir <- tempfile("cornwall-clm-")
dir.create(results_dir)

# Tables for other software
write.csv(
  as.data.frame(clm_known, type = "facilities"),
  file.path(results_dir, "practices.csv"),
  row.names = FALSE
)
write.csv(
  as.data.frame(clm_known, type = "origins"),
  file.path(results_dir, "areas.csv"),
  row.names = FALSE
)

# The whole result
saveRDS(clm_known, file.path(results_dir, "clm_known.rds"))
```

A result read back from the RDS file works like the original, and nothing is
refitted.

```{r reload}
saved <- readRDS(file.path(results_dir, "clm_known.rds"))
coef(saved)
head(as.data.frame(saved, type = "facilities"))
```

```{r cleanup, include = FALSE}
unlink(results_dir, recursive = TRUE)
```

The `utilization` column is each practice's modeled list. Record the spax
version (`packageVersion("spax")`) with saved results.

## Under the hood

`spax()` runs the step functions of the package, which the [Function
map](function-naming.html) lists. For numeric data such as these, `prep_data()`
calls `prepare_allocation()`. `spax()` binds the specification to the data
with `clm_allocation()`, fits it with `fit_allocation()` or, when every
parameter has a value, evaluates it with `evaluate_allocation()`, and
`predict()` calls `predict_allocation()`. The result keeps the bound model
(`clm$model`) and the fit (`clm$fit`). `fit_allocation()` and
`evaluate_allocation()` take the bound model, and `predict_allocation()`
accepts the result itself.
